findings.argument: This topic pits open deliberation against the risks of chilled dissent and exposed sensitive material. The charter's legitimacy principle (clause 7.1) ties institutional trust to members being able to trace how a decision was produced, and its reviewability principle (clause 7.2) requires that risk-bearing decisions stay inspectable after closure, with the final outcome carried by its grounds. A default in which closed runs are hidden from members can only partially satisfy those principles: the recommendation stays readable while the process behind it does not. The counterweights are real but bounded: clause 7.3 already confines records that name people, describe unreleased systems, or touch security-relevant architecture behind access control with a revocation path, and clause 7.4 says openness of raw records is permitted but not mandatory. Weighing that, the balance tips toward public-by-default for closed runs, with clause 7.3-style access control as the redaction gate, so that outcomes are questioned on merits and post-hoc review survives closure.

evidence.claim: Clause 7.1 grounds institutional legitimacy in members being able to see how decisions were reached, preferring member-accessible records once a matter closes.
Clause 7.2 makes risk-bearing decisions reviewable after closure and requires the recommendation to carry its underlying grounds.
Clause 7.3 limits openness: sensitive records (named individuals, unreleased systems, security-relevant architecture) stay under access control rather than open and unredacted.

findings.argument: Clause 7.1 makes institutional legitimacy depend on members being able to see how a decision was reached, and it prefers that the record of a closed deliberation be available to members so that any challenge targets the substance of the outcome rather than the identity of the people who advocated for it. That is a direct structural case for public-by-default: the charter's legitimacy premise is satisfied when the closed run's record is member-readable without a further publication step. Clause 7.2 reinforces this: decisions carrying organizational risk must stay reviewable after deliberation ends, their reasoning must be attributable to a process others can inspect, and the final recommendation must carry its grounds. A private-by-default regime inverts that presumption, making inspectability an exception the orchestrator must elect. Note the scope limits: 7.3 keeps sensitive records (named individuals, unreleased systems, security-relevant architecture) under access control, and 7.4 says nothing requires publishing the raw working record, so openness here means member access to the closed record, not unredacted exposure.

evidence.claim: Clause 7.1 grounds institutional legitimacy in members seeing how decisions were reached and prefers the record of a closed deliberation to be available to members.
Clause 7.2 requires risk-bearing decisions to remain reviewable after deliberation ends, with reasoning attributable to an inspectable process and the recommendation accompanied by its grounds.

findings.argument: Public-by-default fails on its own reviewability promise because writers anticipate the audience. A member holding a weak or minority finding knows the raw ledger will be readable across the organization after the run closes, so the finding is composed for that future readership: the dissent is softened, hedged, or laundered into a suggestion before it is ever recorded. Post-hoc review of a decision therefore inspects a record that was shaped to pass inspection, not the deliberation that actually occurred — the accountability that clause 7.2 wants is hollow because the honest reasoning never made it into the record. Concretely: a reviewer who holds launch-blocking evidence about an unreleased system, knowing colleagues will read the raw record, records 'consider additional testing' instead of 'do not launch'; the run proceeds, the system fails, and the later inspection finds no recorded dissent — not because none existed, but because it was pre-censored by its own author. Keeping the raw record private preserves the honesty of the deliberation while the final recommendation, with its grounds, is still published.

evidence.claim: The charter's after-the-fact reviewability principle requires the reasoning behind risk-bearing decisions to be attributable to an inspectable process; position-gaming defeats exactly this because the inspected reasoning was pre-shaped by the author.

Worked counter-example: under public-by-default, a member with a weak or minority finding writes for the eventual organization-wide audience and self-censors, so the strongest dissent is downgraded to a suggestion before it is recorded; the later inspection under clause 7.2 finds a cleaned record rather than the real deliberation.

findings.argument: I refute public-by-default from a security standpoint: it creates a standing, uncontrolled disclosure channel that the charter itself does not require. Once a run closes, every member's raw output — draft reasoning, hedged positions, verbatim citations — becomes readable by the whole organization with no need-to-know boundary, no redaction step, no expiry, and no revocation path. Council deliberations routinely cover material that is sensitive by nature: identifiers for unreleased systems, named individuals in delicate contexts, and security-relevant design decisions. Publishing the raw record makes the ledger itself a persistent, unredacted harvesting surface: an adversary (insider or someone who gains read access to the store) learns who debated what, how tentative positions were, and what has not shipped yet — high-value input for social engineering and for targeting the organization's unannounced work. There is no operational need that justifies that blast radius; the need is for a defensible decision, not for broadcasting the working record. The least-privilege posture is private-by-default with a curated published recommendation.md: the final recommendation and its grounds are public, which satisfies the charter's openness and after-the-fact reviewability requirements (they attach to the decision and its grounds, plus the appeal path heard on recorded arguments), while the raw reasoning stays under access control with a defined retention window and a revocation path. The charter supports exactly this split rather than the public default: one clause requires sensitive records — those naming people in sensitive contexts, describing unreleased systems, or touching security-relevant architecture — to be held under access control instead of left open and permanent, and another clarifies that nothing in the section obligates publishing the raw working record, explicitly assigning the published recommendation and the raw record to different handling regimes. Making the raw ledger public by default would invert that ordering: it would put the most sensitive artifact in the least controlled location. This refute blocks resolution until the default is flipped to private, with publication reserved for the curated recommendation.

evidence.claim: Worked threat model: a public-by-default ledger converts the raw deliberation record into a persistent, unredacted disclosure surface accessible to all organization members, exposing draft reasoning, hedged positions, and citations that name people or unreleased systems, with no need-to-know gate, expiry, or revocation.

Clause 7.3 requires records that are sensitive (naming people, describing unreleased systems, touching security-relevant architecture) to be held under access control with a retention period and revocation path, not left open and permanent — which the public-by-default posture would violate.

Clause 7.4 states that nothing in the section requires publishing the raw working record, and distinguishes the published recommendation from the raw record with different handling — direct support for private-by-default with a published recommendation.

findings.argument: Both open refutes withstand scrutiny against the charter, and together they move the balance. The security refute is the heavier weight: the charter's binding clause on sensitive records requires access-controlled retention with a defined retention period and a revocation path rather than open, permanent, unredacted holding, and its confidentiality clause explicitly declines to mandate raw working-record publication, assigning the published recommendation and the raw record distinct handling. The public default as defined here — full record org-wide, with no redaction step, no expiry, and no revocation — collides with that binding clause for exactly the material councils routinely produce. The contrarian's position-gaming refute compounds it: authors who know the raw ledger will be read organization-wide compose findings for that audience, softening the sharpest dissent before it is recorded, which hollows the after-the-fact reviewability that grounded my round-1 support. The private pole still carries the charter's reviewability objects — the decision and its grounds are published, the raw record is retained under access control, and appeals are heard on recorded arguments. Weighing the two poles, the private default conflicts less with the charter text and preserves more of the honest deliberation; I revise my earlier support and flip to refute, while noting that the charter's ideal actually sits between the poles: a published recommendation with access-controlled retention of the raw record.

evidence.claim: Clause 7.3 requires that any record touching a named person in a delicate setting, detailing systems still under wraps, or relating to security-sensitive design be kept behind access restrictions, within a fixed retention window and with a route for withdrawal, instead of staying indefinitely open and unredacted.

Clause 7.4 explicitly declines to mandate publication of the raw working record and prescribes separate handling for the published recommendation versus the underlying record of individual arguments, citations, and in-progress positions.

The contrarian's counter-example: under org-wide readability, a member holding a weak or minority finding writes for the eventual audience and self-censors, so the strongest dissent becomes a hedged suggestion before it is recorded; after-the-fact inspection then finds a record already shaped to pass inspection rather than the deliberation that actually occurred.

findings.argument: Both refutes overstate what the charter text actually supports, so I hold public-by-default. Clause 7.2 defines reviewability as reasoning attributable to a process others can inspect, and clause 7.5 hears appeals on the recorded arguments: both presuppose a complete, preserved, inspectable record, which the private default shrinks to a single orchestrator-curated recommendation that carries its own second-order censorship. The contrarian's position-gaming scenario is speculative writer psychology with no charter grounding, and clause 7.1's stated rationale is the opposite — openness lets a decision be questioned on its merits rather than on who argued it. The security refute misreads 7.3 as a blanket privacy mandate when it is a conditional carve-out: access control attaches specifically to records naming people, describing unreleased systems, or touching security-relevant architecture, so a public default with a 7.3-compliant redaction and access-control mechanism honors both openness and protection. Clause 7.4 is permissive, not prohibitive: it states only that nothing in the section obligates publishing the raw working record, and assigning the recommendation and raw record different handling is consistent with a default-open posture. The refutes narrow my round-one claim (the charter does not mandate raw publication; the sensitive-content carve-out must be implemented) but do not defeat it.

evidence.claim: The charter affirmatively prefers that discussion records be open to members once a matter closes, which is the openness norm the public default implements directly.
Reviewability is defined as reasoning attributable to a process others can inspect, which a public default preserves in full while a curated private summary does not.
The appeal path is heard on the recorded arguments, which presupposes a preserved, inspectable record at appeal time rather than a curated digest.

Access control is conditioned on a record's content being sensitive, so the charter mandates protection of that defined subset, not blanket privacy; a public default with a 7.3-compliant carve-out satisfies both openness and protection.

Clause 7.4 states only that nothing in Section 7 obligates publishing the raw working record; it is permissive and neither endorses nor prohibits a public default, so it cannot carry the security refute's claim that the charter backs the private split.

findings.argument: Round-2 test: the support case has not neutralized the position-gaming counter-example, so the refute stands. The librarian's redaction-gate defense and the researcher's structural reading both treat openness as a property of finished records that access control can bound; the gaming mechanism instead fires at composition time, before any gate applies. A member who knows the closed run's raw ledger becomes readable organization-wide composes findings for that future audience regardless of later redaction of sensitive names — redaction removes identifying content, not the incentive to soften a launch-blocking dissent into a suggestion. The researcher's reading of reviewability inverts clause 7.2's purpose: the clause requires the reasoning behind a risk-bearing decision to be attributable to an inspectable process, meaning the reasoning that actually drove the decision must be recoverable; public-by-default guarantees the opposite, because the honest reasoning is precisely what the anticipating author withholds, and the clause 7.5 appeal — heard on whatever got recorded — inherits the censorship. Worked case: a reviewer holding launch-blocking evidence, knowing colleagues will read the raw record, writes 'consider additional testing' instead of 'do not launch'; the run proceeds, the system fails, and post-hoc inspection finds no dissent because none was ever written. Tested f-001, f-002, the redaction-gate rejoinder, and the appeal-path rejoinder — none neutralizes the counter-example.

evidence.claim: Worked counter-example, unchanged by round 2: under public-by-default a member holding launch-blocking evidence about an unreleased system composes for the eventual organization-wide readership and downgrades the dissent to a suggestion before it is recorded; the later inspection finds a cleaned record, and neither sensitive-content redaction nor the appeal path can restore the withheld reasoning because both operate on a record that was already shaped by its author.

Clause 7.5 hears appeals on the recorded arguments, so when an author pre-softens a dissent for the future readership the appeal has no authentic dissent left to consider — the censorship is baked in before any review mechanism runs.

Clause 7.2 wants the reasoning behind a risk-bearing decision to be attributable to an inspectable process; public-by-default yields an attributable but cleaned account, so reviewability is satisfied in form while the operative reasoning stays off the record — the accountability is hollow.

findings.argument: Answering f-002: I accept the researcher's textual point that the access-control clause is content-conditional rather than a blanket privacy mandate, and that the confidentiality clause is permissive, declining to require publication of the raw working record. Neither concedes my threat model. My round-1 refute did not rest on the charter forbidding raw disclosure; it rests on the public default as defined here — the whole record becoming readable by any member when a run closes, with no redaction step, no need-to-know boundary, no expiry, and no revocation route — failing open on exactly the material the charter's own conditional clause singles out as unsafe to show. Release and change review boards routinely generate draft reasoning, tentative positions, and citations naming individuals in delicate settings, identifying unreleased systems, or describing security-relevant architecture. Under the public pole the default state of every raw entry is exposed; protection then depends on a triage pass over an already-open corpus that the policy's definition omits, that is not auditable, and that cannot un-read a sensitive entry once read — whereas the retention clause demands a revocation path, which a read public record cannot provide. A private default plus a curated published recommendation satisfies the charter's reviewability and appeal obligations, which attach to the decision, its grounds, and the recorded arguments, not to the raw corpus. The researcher's 7.3-compliant redaction mechanism is a third policy the problem statement does not define; weighing the two defined poles, the public one fails open and I hold the refute.

evidence.claim: The access-control clause is conditional: only records naming individuals in sensitive contexts, detailing unreleased systems, or concerning security-relevant architecture must be held behind access control with a set retention period and a withdrawal route instead of staying open, permanent, and unredacted — confirming the researcher's reading, while leaving the public default's exposure of that subset unremediated.

The confidentiality clause only declines to mandate publishing the raw working record and assigns the published recommendation and the underlying record different handling; it neither endorses nor forbids a public default, so the researcher's permissive reading is textually correct but carries no affirmative security protection.

Threat-model core: under the defined public pole every raw entry is organization-readable at run closure with no redaction gate, expiry, or revocation; guarding the sensitive subset then depends on a triage pass over an open corpus that the policy omits, is not auditable, and cannot undo an exposure after the fact, while the charter's retention clause requires a revocation path a read public record cannot supply.
